intuition: For each possible length, remember the smallest ending value of an increasing subsequence seen so far. A smaller ending is easier to extend with future values. Use binary search to replace the first saved ending that is at least the current number, or append a new ending.

Among equally long increasing subsequences, the one with the smaller final value is always at least as useful. Any future value that extends a larger tail also extends the smaller one. Keep the minimum known tail for each achievable length, allowing less useful endings to be replaced.

These minimum tails are sorted, so binary search locates the length that the next number can improve. Replacing a tail does not destroy an achievable length; it supplies a better ending for that length. Appending adds a new achievable length. The summary array itself need not describe one actual subsequence.

For nums=[3,5,6,2,4], the final tails are [2,4,6]. Their input indices are 3,4,2, so those entries cannot be one subsequence. The length three remains valid because [3,5,6] was achieved earlier; each stored tail certifies its own length independently.

steps: Reading 10 creates tails=[10]. Reading 9 replaces its first entry, and reading 2 replaces it again: tails=[2].
Value 5 is greater than every tail, so append it: tails=[2,5].
Value 3 replaces the first tail at least 3, producing [2,3]; length 2 remains achievable with a better ending.
Values 7 and 101 extend the summary to [2,3,7,101], representing achievable lengths 1 through 4.
Value 18 replaces 101, leaving [2,3,7,18]. The final summary length, 4, is the answer.

concept.question: Why is a smaller ending value a better representative of the same subsequence length?
intuition: Listing all subsequences grows exponentially. Keeping just one arbitrary subsequence can also discard a more extendable alternative of the same length.

For each achievable length, remember the smallest ending value among increasing subsequences of that length. A smaller ending is easier for a future value to exceed. Find the first ending no smaller than the new value and replace it; append if the new value exceeds every ending.
concept.observation: Replace the first ending at least as large as the new value; equality must not increase a strictly increasing length.
approach: Keep the smallest ending for each attainable length.
Locate the first ending no smaller than the new value.
Replace it or append a new attainable length; return the number of saved lengths.
concept.correctness: A new value can extend any shorter subsequence whose smallest ending is below it. Replacing the first ending no smaller than that value gives the smallest possible ending for the corresponding length without changing longer feasible lengths. Appending occurs exactly when one longer increasing subsequence becomes achievable. The summary length is therefore the maximum increasing length.

complexity.explanation: Locate each replacement with a logarithmic search through the ordered ending summary. Total work is linear-times-logarithmic, and summary memory can grow linearly.

pitfalls: Replace the first ending at least as large as the new value; equality must not increase a strictly increasing length.
